chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from an-Nadr from 'Asim ibn Humayd from Muhammad ibn Qays from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

He gave a ruling concerning a man who freed a male slave and stipulated his walayah (manumission bond), then the one who freed him died, and he had no children except women. Then the mawla (freed slave) died and left wealth, and he had 'asabah (agnates). The daughters of his master and the 'asabah disputed his inheritance. So he ruled that the inheritance belongs to the 'asabah who pay his diyyah (blood money), if a incident occurs in which there is diyyah.

key_terms.عَصَبَة: Asabah: Agnatic male relatives who inherit the residue of an estate after fixed shares are distributed.
key_terms.عَقْل: Aql: In this context, the collective liability for paying diyyah (blood money) of the deceased.
key_terms.وَلَاء: Walayah: The bond of manumission linking a freed slave to his former master, often entailing inheritance rights.

ai.seo_question: Who inherits a freed slave's estate when the master's family consists only of women and the master had agnates?
ai.summary: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) ruled that when a man frees a slave and stipulates the walayah bond, upon the master's death (leaving only female descendants) and subsequently the freed slave's death, the inheritance of the freed slave goes to the 'asabah (agnatic male relatives) who are responsible for paying his diyyah, rather than the female descendants or other heirs. This ruling highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle that the right of inheritance (mirath) is contingent upon the obligation of diyyah (blood money), a distinction often debated in contrast to Sunni schools where walayah alone may suffice for inheritance. The case underscores the specific legal mechanism by which the freedman's lineage connects to his former master's family for inheritance purposes when direct male heirs are absent.
